label: Claude Opus 5.5
output:
**4 out of 5 stars: a real upgrade for a small church, with a few honest caveats**

Our congregation livestreamed worship on a webcam from 2020 until last winter, when we finally replaced it with the Lindqvist PT-20. We bought it from Chancel AV in February 2026 for $2,140, plus $95 for the wall mount. I'm a pastor, not an engineer, so take this as a review from someone who has learned more about cameras this year than he ever planned to. I'm writing it mainly for other small parishes trying to decide whether this is worth money they may not have.

**Our setup**

Our nave is 92 feet long, and the camera is mounted on the balcony rail at the back. It runs on PoE, so a single cable goes up to the balcony and carries both power and video. That alone saved us a lot of trouble. We use the NDI output into OBS on an old office PC and stream to our YouTube channel, where we usually have 30 to 60 viewers on a Sunday. It also has a plain HDMI output if you'd rather go that way.

We have nine presets saved: altar, pulpit, lectern, font, choir loft, piano, a wide shot, and two for the chancel steps. Our 16-year-old acolyte, Erik, runs everything from the free web app on a tablet. He learned it in one afternoon. If your volunteers aren't technical, that matters more than any spec sheet.

**Picture quality**

The 20x optical zoom really does reach from the back of a long nave. On the webcam, people at the front were small blurry shapes. Now we can get a clean, close shot of the pulpit or the font from 92 feet away. The 1080p60 picture is sharp and smooth.

The moment that sold me came from Delores, one of our homebound members, who is 82. She called to say she could finally read the hymn numbers on the board. That was the whole reason we did this.

Low light was the other test. At the Easter Vigil in April, the first "Christ the Lord Is Risen Today" was sung by candlelight alone. The picture got grainy, but it stayed usable, and you could see what was happening. Our old webcam would have shown nothing but dots. Don't expect miracles in a dark church, but this camera holds up far better than a webcam does.

**What didn't go perfectly**

On our first Sunday the presets drifted a few degrees by the time we reached the sermon. Firmware update 2.4 in March fixed that, and we haven't had the problem since. If you buy one, update the firmware before you rely on it.

The autofocus hunts when someone walks between the camera and the pulpit, which happens a lot in a working church. We now lock focus on our presets, and that solved it. It's an easy fix once you know about it.

The manual is thin and badly translated. I would have been stuck without Chancel AV's tech support. Marcy walked me through several things on the phone, patiently and clearly, and she was excellent. Their support was a big part of why this went well for us.

**What it won't fix**

This one is important. **The camera does nothing for your sound.** Audio isn't the camera's job, and it didn't help our sound problem at all. If your online viewers mostly complain that they can't hear, a better camera won't fix that, and you might be better off spending the money on audio first. Better video did make our audio problems more noticeable, if anything.

**Is it worth it?**

For us, yes. I'd buy it again. The zoom, the low-light performance, the single cable, and how easy it is for a teenager to run have all made our livestream better for the people who depend on it.

The reason it's four stars and not five: the early preset drift, the autofocus behavior, and the weak manual. Also, at this price, I'd tell a congregation under 100 people to think carefully. Depending on your building and what you need, you might do fine with something cheaper. If your sanctuary is long, your lighting is dim, and you have members at home who really need to see what's going on, the PT-20 earns its price.

— A Lutheran pastor in Minneapolis
